text:
Your team uses AI. So why are you doing more of their work?

@tobi  calls it the “slop grenade.”

Someone asks AI to make a deck. They don't review the deck. They send it to you.

Now you're the one trying to understand the recommendation, untangle the wording, check the numbers, and rebuild the slides.

They got a faster first draft. You got another job.

@neilpatel  and I talked about this on Marketing School. We got into bad handoffs, generic design, ad campaigns that nobody supervises, and why using AI doesn't remove the need to think.

I've been pushing my team to use AI. I want people to get better at it. But I don't want “I used AI” to become an explanation for work that the person sending it hasn't even read.

I'm not exempt, either. In this conversation, I call out the default AI design choices I saw at an event—including in my own presentation.

1. Start with the handoff

The slop grenade is a handoff problem.

The first person sees a completed file. The second person discovers all the unfinished thinking inside it.

A deck has slides. A document has headings. A campaign has ads. There may even be a confident conclusion at the end.

But if the person who made it can't explain the recommendation, defend the important claims, or connect it to the brief, the person receiving it has to do that work.

Here's a hypothetical example.

You ask someone for a short proposal about which customer segment to focus on next quarter. They send 20 slides describing five segments, their broad characteristics, and a list of potential channels.

There is no recommendation. No explanation of the tradeoff. No connection to your team's capacity.

You didn't ask for a list of things that could be true. You asked for help making a decision.

The AI may have done exactly what it was prompted to do. The work still isn't ready for the handoff.

Before sending it, the owner needs to ask: “What does the person receiving this need to understand or decide?”

Then check whether the deliverable actually helps them do that.

2. Count the work after generation

It's easy to see the time saved when a draft appears quickly.

The time spent repairing it is less visible. It can sit in comments, extra meetings, follow-up messages, or a manager rewriting the whole thing after everyone else has moved on.

That makes “I made this in five minutes” an incomplete account of what happened.

For a useful comparison, I'd look at the full path:

The brief. The first draft. The owner's review. The recipient's review. The revisions. The point where someone can actually use the work.

Sometimes AI will make that whole path much faster. Sometimes a quick draft will create a long cleanup process. You need to look at the result to know which happened.

I'd rather receive a short recommendation that someone has checked than a large document that makes me discover its problems from scratch.

That doesn't mean every draft has to be perfect. Early collaboration is useful. If you want help thinking through a rough idea, say that clearly.

“Here's an early direction. I need your input on this tradeoff before I build it out” is a different request from “Here's the finished deck.”

Both are legitimate. Confusing them is where people start doing each other's work without agreeing to it.

3. AI is an intelligence amplifier

In the episode, I use a phrase from our friend Syed: “AI is an intelligence amplifier.”

All will be revealed.

When someone brings clear thinking and good judgment to the work, AI can help them explore and produce more. When the thinking is weak or the review is missing, more output can make the problem more obvious.

I don't take that as a permanent label on a person. The useful question is what they do with the tool on this task.

Did they notice that the headline made no sense? Did they compare the options? Did they see that the recommendation didn't answer the question?

Those are opportunities to exercise judgment. Skipping them is a choice about the work process.

One of the examples I discuss is reading an AI-generated deck and starting to question my own understanding because the wording is so strange.

You reread the sentence. You try to work out whether you've missed something. Eventually you realize the sentence itself doesn't make sense.

That is a bad use of the recipient's time.

Before asking another person to decode a slide, try explaining it aloud in one ordinary sentence. If you can't, go back to the idea. A prettier layout won't resolve a confused recommendation.

4. The default design is only a starting point

I describe seeing the same kinds of AI design choices across presentations: familiar layouts, little pills, italic text, and similar ways of framing the message.

And I admit that I was using those choices too.

The point isn't that one visual element is always bad. Three columns can be useful. Italics can be useful. A common layout can be the clearest way to show something.

The problem is accepting the default without asking whether it fits the idea or helps the audience.

If every presentation comes out with the same structure, the same verbal habits, and the same visual emphasis, where does your actual point of view show up?

I'd start a design review with the message:

What is the one thing this slide needs to communicate?

What deserves the most attention?

What can we remove?

Is the audience supposed to compare options, understand a process, or believe a claim?

Those are different jobs. They shouldn't all receive the same treatment because the tool happened to produce it first.

If the slide is about a real result, show the relevant evidence. If it's about a choice, make the choice clear. If you need three minutes to explain a decorative headline, rewrite the headline.

AI gives you something to work with. You still have to decide what belongs in the final version.

5. Review your own work before asking someone else to review it

We discuss a story about a boss asking: “Is this your best piece of work?”

I like the question because it forces an honest pause before the handoff.

Neil pushes back on the idea of having to ask it repeatedly. His expectation is that people should already be checking their work before they send it.

That's a useful distinction. A manager can establish the standard, but the process can't depend on the manager reminding everyone to care every single time.

I'd turn that into a simple personal check:

Have I read the whole thing?

Have I checked the claims that matter?

Have I removed the parts that don't help?

Can I explain why I recommend this version?

Have I said where I still need input?

The last question is important. Reviewing your own work doesn't require pretending you know everything.

It can mean saying, “I checked these three inputs. This assumption is still uncertain. Here's how it affects the recommendation.”

That is useful work. It gives the next person a clear place to focus.

What isn't useful is making them discover every uncertainty themselves because you forwarded the first output and moved on.

6. Define what good work looks like

A vague instruction to “make it better” leaves too much room for interpretation.

If you're leading the team, be specific about the job the work needs to do.

For a proposal, that might mean a clear recommendation, the reasons behind it, the assumptions that matter, and the next decision.

For a piece of content, it might mean a strong opening, a useful idea, accurate examples, and a payoff that matches the promise.

For a campaign, it might mean a stated objective, a defined audience, approved creative, and a plan for checking what happens after launch.

I'd also show examples and explain why they work. “This is good” is less useful than “This makes the recommendation obvious, shows the supporting evidence, and gives the reader a clear next step.”

Then ask people to use those same questions in their own review.

The aim is to help the person sending the work make better decisions before the handoff. If every quality decision still has to happen in the manager's head, the team hasn't learned the standard yet.

You don't need a huge manual for each task. You need enough shared understanding that people can tell the difference between a draft and work that's ready to use.

7. Don't confuse a brainstorm with a company policy

In the conversation, I float a possible response to repeated slop grenades: delaying my next review and making the missed handoff visible.

I explicitly say we're brainstorming possible solutions. Neil offers his own view on warnings and accountability, and he says he's not in HR.

That context matters.

I'm not presenting that exchange here as a finished policy to copy into your employee handbook. The useful management question is how to address a pattern of unchecked work instead of quietly absorbing it forever.

My practical starting point would be much simpler: describe the specific problem, make the expected standard clear, and make sure the person understands how to meet it.

Was the brief unclear? Did they lack the information? Did they misunderstand the review stage? Or did they simply skip a review they knew they needed to do?

Those situations deserve different conversations.

For actual employment procedures or consequences, use the people responsible for those decisions in your organization. A podcast brainstorm isn't a substitute for that work.

What I do want to avoid is a repeating pattern where the same person sends unchecked work, someone else fixes it, and nobody addresses why it keeps happening.

Fixing the file is sometimes necessary. It doesn't automatically fix the process that produced it.

8. A review tool can help with a defined question

We also talk about Jev, which I describe as a classifier.

One possible use I discuss is reviewing content against guidelines and checking for duplication before a person has to review it.

The important word is “possible.” Talking through a workflow isn't proof that the workflow will catch every issue or improve every piece of content.

I'd start with questions that are specific enough to act on.

Does this draft address the promised topic?

Does it repeat something we've already published?

Is a claim missing its supporting evidence?

Does the draft conflict with a stated content guideline?

Those are more useful starting points than asking for one unexplained quality score and treating the number as the final answer.

If a check flags something, a person should inspect the actual passage and decide what to do. If the evidence is missing, the system should show that gap instead of guessing.

And if the tool says the draft looks fine, that still doesn't tell you how a video sounds, whether a visual blocks the screen, or whether the final export feels good to watch.

Different parts of the work need different kinds of review.

9. Compare the draft with the brief

One review habit I'd use across almost any kind of work is putting the original request next to the proposed answer.

It sounds obvious. It's also easy to skip once a polished draft exists.

Suppose the brief is: “Help a new customer understand the first step.”

A generated answer might explain the entire product, list every feature, introduce three future use cases, and finish with a broad call to action.

That may contain useful material. It still may not make the first step clear.

Or suppose the brief asks for three distinct packaging concepts. Three versions of the same title with slightly different wording may not give you three different ways to position the idea.

Review the work against the request, rather than against the amount of effort that appears to have gone into it.

I'd ask the owner to name the intended audience, the desired outcome, and the constraint that mattered most.

Then point to where the draft serves each one.

If they can't do that, there may be a problem with the brief or the draft. Either way, it's better to find it before the work moves further downstream.

The tool doesn't know which requirement you forgot to include. The person responsible for the deliverable has to keep the actual job in view.

10. Check the claims that carry the recommendation

Not every sentence has the same importance.

A typo in a low-stakes internal note is different from an unsupported number that drives a budget decision.

I'd focus verification on the claims the recommendation depends on.

Where did the number come from? What period does it cover? Is it revenue, profit, spend, or a forecast? Are two numbers being compared on the same basis?

If you're using a customer's words, did you preserve what they meant? If you're summarizing a source, did you keep the qualification that changes the conclusion?

These questions apply whether AI helped produce the draft or a person wrote it from scratch.

AI makes it easier to create fluent language. Fluency doesn't answer the questions above.

For an uncertain claim, there are several honest options: verify it, qualify it, remove it, or identify it as an open question.

The wrong move is leaving it in as a confident statement because it makes the document sound stronger.

A reviewer should be able to tell which facts are established, which are estimates, and which are the author's judgment.

That separation gives them a better basis for deciding. It also makes revisions easier because they can challenge the specific assumption instead of trying to reverse-engineer the whole argument.

11. Neil's ad-campaign story is about supervision

Neil tells a story about a company that used AI to help manage its ads and then blamed the tool for poor performance.

He recalls roughly 112,000 Canadian dollars in spend and only around 3,000–4,000 Canadian dollars in revenue. He also makes rough U.S.-dollar conversions in the conversation.

These are approximate figures from his account, not an independently audited campaign case study.

The detail I care about most is the timing. According to Neil, the campaign ran for roughly 40 days before the person checked it.

His response is direct: you set it up, you were responsible for it, and you needed to supervise it.

Changing tools may or may not improve a campaign. It doesn't explain why nobody checked what the campaign was doing for that long.

If you own a campaign, ownership includes what happens after launch.

What are you looking at? When are you looking at it? What result would make you investigate? Who can pause or change the work?

The answers depend on the campaign and the business. The principle is that they need to exist before you discover a large problem.

I'd ask those questions even if the work were being done by a person. Adding AI doesn't make them disappear.

12. “The AI did it” doesn't settle responsibility

A tool can produce a bad result. A person can configure it poorly. The brief can be wrong. The monitoring can be missing. Several of those things can happen at once.

You have to understand what happened before deciding how to fix it.

But “the AI did it” doesn't answer the operational questions.

Who chose the task? Who decided which information to provide? Who accepted the output? Who was supposed to check the result?

In Neil's story, the operator wanted to blame the AI for the campaign. Neil focused on the person's responsibility to supervise the work they had put in motion.

That's the part I'd carry into any team discussion.

If someone uses AI to produce a deliverable, the handoff should still have an owner. There should be a person who can explain the work and respond when something doesn't make sense.

Otherwise the recipient has to become the owner by default.

That is especially frustrating when the recipient thought they were being asked for a final decision, then discovers they are actually being asked to finish the thinking, research, and quality control.

Ownership doesn't mean the person must do every step manually. It means they stay responsible for whether those steps produced something useful.

13. Leadership sets the expectation, too

Neil and I also discuss how responsibility moves up through the organization.

I make the point that a CEO's decisions and expectations affect what happens downstream. Neil qualifies that in a very large organization, a specific campaign issue may be too small to reach the CEO directly.

We don't frame that part identically. It's useful to hear the distinction in the conversation.

For me, the leadership lesson is that pushing people to use AI has to come with a clear standard for the work it produces.

If the message is only “use more AI,” people may reasonably focus on showing how much they use it.

I'd want the message to include: solve the right problem, check the output, and stay accountable for the result.

Those expectations should show up in feedback, too.

If a leader praises the speed of a draft but quietly spends an hour fixing it, the person who sent it may never understand the real cost of that handoff.

Tell them what needed to change and why. Where possible, have them make the revision and explain the decision.

That takes effort. But repeatedly doing the work for someone while hoping they'll infer the standard is a weak way to teach it.

14. Being busy with AI isn't the same as producing results

Neil makes another point I like: someone can get more tasks done while producing fewer useful results if the tasks don't relate to the right goals.

AI can make it easier to stay busy.

You can generate another report, another set of ideas, another version of the deck, another piece of content.

The question is what changed because you did that work.

Did the proposal help the customer decide? Did the content make a useful idea clearer? Did the campaign move toward its objective? Did the analysis change a decision?

Sometimes the answer will take time to observe. That's fine. You can still be clear about what you're trying to achieve and what evidence you'll use.

What I'd avoid is using the volume of AI output as the main proof that the team is improving.

A large pile of drafts can still be a pile of unfinished decisions.

For a recurring task, I'd pick a small number of outcomes worth watching and review them alongside the work required to get there.

If production gets faster but the recipient's cleanup gets longer, I want to know. If review takes a little longer but catches a material mistake, I want to know that too.

15. The thumbnail example is about iteration

Near the end of the episode, I talk about using AI skills to work on my YouTube thumbnails.

The first pass doesn't always work. The second pass doesn't always work. Sometimes I need a third or fourth pass.

I may spend five to 10 minutes going through those changes.

In the conversation, I say that click-through rates on my videos had been around 3.5%–4% and were now around 7%–8%.

That's my reported experience. It isn't a controlled test proving that AI, or one particular revision, caused the difference. Videos, audiences, topics, and packaging can vary.

The useful working habit is that I don't have to accept the first output just because it was produced quickly.

I can look at it, decide what isn't working, and give a specific correction.

Is the promise clear? Can you read the text at a small size? Does the image support the title? Is there too much competing for attention? Does the video actually deliver what the packaging suggests?

Those are judgment calls. AI can help me explore the options, but I still need to make the calls.

I'd apply the same habit to a proposal, an ad, or a piece of writing: review the first pass against the job, then revise the thing that matters most.

16. More workflows will require more judgment

I talk about a future where marketers run several AI-assisted workflows and keep checking whether each one is working.

That's my expectation about how the role may develop. It isn't a guarantee about every marketing job or a precise timeline.

What interests me is the change in where attention goes.

You may spend less time producing every first draft by hand and more time deciding what to ask for, checking the output, diagnosing failures, and choosing what should happen next.

That can be valuable work. It still requires understanding the task.

If you don't know what a good result looks like, it's hard to judge whether an automated process produced one.

And if you set up several processes without a way to review them, you can end up with several places where errors accumulate.

I'd rather see someone run one useful workflow that they understand than ten that they can't explain.

Start with a real problem. Define the expected result. Decide what a person needs to check. Look at what actually happens. Improve it from there.

The skill is being able to connect the tool's output to the business problem and notice when that connection breaks.

17. A practical handoff I'd be happy to receive

Here's a simple format I'd try for work that needs a decision:

“The goal is ___.

I recommend ___ because ___.

I checked ___.

The main tradeoff is ___.

The part I still need help with is ___.

The decision we need now is ___.”

You don't need to fill this out like a form for every message. The point is to make the thinking visible.

If the task is small, two sentences might do it. If it's a consequential proposal, you may need supporting material.

What I want to avoid is opening a file and having to reconstruct the goal, the recommendation, and the unresolved questions from scratch.

The format also helps the person making the work.

If they can't complete “I recommend ___ because ___,” they may have more comparison to do. If they can't say what they checked, they may be handing off too early. If every part needs help, the task may need a different brief or an earlier discussion.

Good handoffs make it easier for the next person to contribute at the right level.

18. What I'd try with a team this week

I wouldn't begin by building a huge new process.

I'd pick one recurring deliverable that often comes back for revisions.

First, get clear about its purpose. Who uses it? What decision or action should it support? What keeps going wrong?

Second, agree on a short review checklist with the people who make and receive it. Include the checks that would have caught the recent problems.

Third, have the owner use that checklist before the next handoff and state any unresolved questions.

Fourth, ask the recipient to give specific feedback instead of silently fixing everything.

Then look at the next few examples. Did the same problem happen again? Did the checklist help? Did it create unnecessary work? Did people become clearer about when to ask for help?

This is a proposed way to test the idea, not a result I'm claiming we've already achieved.

I'd keep the parts that help and revise the parts that don't.

The point is to improve the actual handoff. A checklist that nobody uses, or one that becomes a ritual without catching anything, doesn't solve the problem.

Start small enough that you can inspect the work and learn from what happens.

AI is leverage. You still decide where to apply it.

The closing analogy Neil and I discuss is applying leverage to a good or bad real estate investment. The point in this conversation is amplification: more leverage doesn't turn a weak underlying decision into a strong one.

I think about AI the same way.

Use it to explore, draft, compare, and revise. Use it to save time where it actually helps. But don't confuse the existence of an output with the completion of the job.

Read what you're sending. Check what matters. Own the recommendation. Stay involved after the work goes live.

If you're the leader, make the standard visible and give people specific feedback. If you're the person making the work, don't wait for your manager to perform the review you could have done yourself.

And if you need help, ask for it clearly. There is a big difference between bringing someone a thoughtful question and handing them a slop grenade.

Where does the cleanup land on your team—with the person using AI, or with the person receiving it?

[1/n] Introducing Diffusion Reward Models (DRM)

Reward Models are at the core of LLM post-training. But almost all of them make the same simplification:
they collapse human preference into a single score.

The problem is that human feedback is often not a point — different people can hold distinct, even conflicting, judgments about the same response.

So we asked: Can a Reward Model learn the distribution of human preference?

Here’s what we found 👇

📄 Paper: https://t.co/e0EMNa3I64
💻 Code: https://t.co/KVosB5D5PI
🤗 Models: https://t.co/wwdDpOtgbL

[2/n] Our answer is DRM: model rewards as distributions.

Instead of predicting a scalar, DRM replaces the conventional value head with a lightweight Diffusion Reward Head.

Given a prompt-response pair, it generates samples from the reward distribution.

So disagreement, uncertainty, and multiple plausible judgments can remain in the reward itself, rather than being averaged away.

And the same framework works with both multi-attribute rewards and pairwise preferences.
